clinical_category: Postural drainage and manual chest physiotherapy - secretion mobilization technique
blueprint_topic: Supportive airway-clearance positioning and comfort-focused respiratory care
stem: A client with retained respiratory secretions is receiving postural drainage as part of an individualized airway-clearance plan. Which description of the technique is accurate?

options.A: The client is positioned so gravity can help move secretions from targeted lung regions toward larger airways; manual percussion or vibration may be added when appropriate
options.B: The client remains in one neutral position because body position has no relationship to the lung region being drained
options.C: Coughing is suppressed during and after treatment so mobilized secretions remain in the smaller airways
options.D: Postural drainage is a universal routine treatment for every respiratory condition regardless of secretion retention, tolerance, or contraindications

rationale: A is correct. Current NCBI/StatPearls guidance describes postural drainage as positioning the body to use gravity to move mucus from specific lung regions toward larger airways. Manual chest physiotherapy can include percussion and vibration to loosen and mobilize retained secretions, and coughing or deep breathing may be used to help expel mobilized mucus. B ignores the segment-specific role of positioning. C is opposite to the goal of secretion clearance. D is incorrect because airway-clearance techniques require individualized selection based on secretion burden, clinical condition, tolerance, and contraindications.
educational_objective: Describe postural drainage as individualized, gravity-assisted positioning that mobilizes retained secretions toward larger airways and may be combined with percussion, vibration, breathing, and coughing techniques when clinically appropriate.
source_version_date: StatPearls; last update 2024-06-08; current 2026 NCBI Bookshelf edition accessed 2026-08-18
source_locator: NCBI Bookshelf 'Postural Drainage and Vibration' → Introduction: postural drainage positions the body to use gravity to drain mucus from specific lung areas; vibration applies rhythmic pressure to loosen mucus. Technique or Treatment → Manual Chest Physiotherapy: percussion loosens/mobilizes mucus; different positions facilitate drainage from different lung segments; gravity assists movement toward larger airways; deep breathing and coughing may help expel loosened secretions. Contraindications/Indications: technique selection is individualized and should account for clinical status and contraindications.
source_claim_supported: Current NCBI/StatPearls content directly supports gravity-based segmental positioning, optional manual percussion/vibration, and cough/breathing maneuvers as components of individualized secretion-clearance therapy.
blueprint_source_organization: National Council of State Boards of Nursing (NCSBN)
blueprint_locator: Basic Care and Comfort client-needs subcategory (6–12% of items), within Physiological Integrity; this item tests supportive respiratory-care positioning and secretion-management measures tailored to client comfort and tolerance.
correction_summary: Substantive rebuild. AARC currently lists its older Postural Drainage Therapy guideline as retired, so the source item could not retain that guideline as current authority. The final item uses current NCBI/StatPearls guidance and limits the claim to the directly supported mechanics and individualized use of postural drainage and manual chest physiotherapy, without overstating comparative efficacy.
audit_findings: The source item's AARC postural-drainage guideline is currently listed by AARC as retired and therefore failed the currentness gate.
Current NCBI/StatPearls content directly supports gravity-based targeted positioning and the optional use of percussion/vibration to mobilize mucus.
The final item avoids claiming that manual chest physiotherapy is universally superior to other airway-clearance techniques or indicated for every patient.
Distractors test incorrect neutral positioning, cough suppression, and universal routine use; none is defensible.
Independent adversarial second pass found one uniquely correct answer, no unsupported treatment frequency, no second answer, no cueing, and no unresolved conflict.
